metadata.title: Field v. Mans, 516 U.S. 59 (1995) (No. 94-967)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Field v. Mans

Opinion filed: 1995-11-28

Docket No.: 94-967

Citations:
• 133 L. Ed. 2d 351
• 116 S. Ct. 437
• 516 U.S. 59
• 1995 U.S. LEXIS 8312

Case holding summaries:
• holding that the creditor must prove justifiable reliance
• "The more apparently deliberate the contrast, the stronger the inference, as applied, for example, to contrasting statutory sections originally enacted simultaneously in relevant respects."
• the U.S. Supreme Court discussed the applicability of the duty when there are suspicious circumstances, but did not discuss whether or how the duty arises by virtue of the creditor's background
• creditor's reliance must be justifiable, but not necessarily reasonable
• stating that level of required prudence depends on whether the recipient of a representation is unwary
• stating that requirement depends on experience and resourcefulness of relying party
• referring to reasonable prudence and diligence, but defining it as depending on intelligence, age, experience, mental and physical condition of the parties, their respective knowledge, and their means of knowledge
• "[I]f it appears that one party has been guilty of an intentional and deliberate fraud, the doctrine is well settled that he cannot defend against such fraud by saying that the same might have been discovered had the party whom he deceived exercised reasonable diligence and care"
• stating that no investigation is necessary for reliance to be justified
• indicating that level of reliance depends on sophistication of parties
• finding right to rely without investigation
• holding that one to whom a representation is made has the right to rely without any further inquiry
• stating that actual reliance is sufficient, notwithstanding relying party's failure to investigate or verify
• stating that, if purchaser is given information that would excite suspicions of reasonably prudent man, he has a duty to investigate
• stating that a representee must be "`justified in relying' " on the misrepresentation
• holding that purchaser had no duty to investigate where seller made clear factual representation
• rejecting reasonable person standard and applying subjective test based on intelligence and experience of aggrieved person
• finding no duty to investigate
• holding that a representee has some duty, although less than a duty to exercise reasonable care, to protect his interest
• requiring justifiable reliance and distinguishing it from reasonable reliance
• holding that purchaser had no duty to investigate
• stating that actual reliance is sufficient, even if plaintiff might have discovered the wrong but for his own neglect
• stating that purchaser must show reasonable reliance
• stating that justifiable reliance applies in analogous situation of indemnity based on fraud
• referring to reasonable reliance, but applying standard as preventing seller from saying that buyer ought not to have been so gullible as to trust him, unless the circumstances are such that buyer appears to have known the truth
• stating that neither purchasers' lack of caution in believing a factual misrepresentation nor their failure to make an independent investigation is a defense to their fraud action
• relying on Restatement (First) and W. Prosser, Law of Torts (1941)
• stating that there is no duty to investigate in absence of anything that would arouse suspicion
• relying on Restatement (First) and W. Prosser, Law of Torts (2d ed. 1955), including example of one-eyed horse, in finding that justifiable reliance is appropriate standard
• creditor required to prove that its reliance was reasonable
• stating that test is not what a reasonable and prudent man would have done but whether plaintiff, in the condition he was in, had a right to rely
• stating that a person who commits intentional misrepresentation cannot excuse himself based on the foolishness of the hearer in believing the representation
• relying on Restatement of Torts § 540 (1938) (hereinafter Restatement (First)), which applies the same rule as in Restatement (Second) of Torts § 540 (1976)
• "`[W]here Congress includes particular language in one section of a statute but omits it in another section of the same Act, it is generally presumed that Congress acts intentionally and purposely in the disparate inclusion or exclusion' "
• noting that a single enactment created provisions with language that differed
• “Section 523(a)(2)(B) expressly requires not only reasonable reliance but also reliance itself.”
• cautioning that a contextual inference "should not be elevated to the level of interpretive trump card"
• § 523(a)(2)(A) "requires justifiable, but not reasonable, reliance"
• fraud exists even if the truth could be learned from public records
• "We construe the terms in § 523(a)(2)(A) to incorporate the general common law of torts, the dominant consensus of common-law jurisdictions, rather than the law of any particular State."
• justifiable reliance required under section 523(a)(2)(A)
• Congress generally Cite as: 587 U. S. (2019) 9 Opinion of the Court meant for the Bankruptcy Code to “incorporate the estab- lished meaning” of “terms that have accumulated settled meaning” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• holding that § 523(a)(2)(A) requires justifiable rather than reasonable reliance
• justifiable reliance required under section 523(a)(2)(A)
• cautioning interpretation is to assume that the legislature meant to give that a contextual inference “should not be elevated to the level force to the differential language. See Russello v. United of interpretive trump card”
• discussing the standard of justifiable reliance and citing with favor an excerpt from the Restatement (Second) of Torts that "a person is justified in relying on a representation of fact "
• "The more apparently deliberate the contrast, the stronger the inference, as applied, for example, to contrasting statutory sections originally enacted simultaneously in relevant respects . . ."
• holding that duty to investigate was not a predicate to demonstrating justifiable reliance under § 523(a)(2)(A), discussing Restatement (Second) of Torts § 540 (1976)
• "We construe the terms in 523(a)(2)(A) to incorporate the general common law of torts . . . "
• surveying the common law of fraud as it stood in 1978
